title: Methods and sources
intro: How BORAMAE tests a trend, how often that test raises a false alarm, and where every piece of data and code comes from.

false_alarms.heading: False-alarm check
false_alarms.how: How the check works: for each value of r₁, the lag-1 autocorrelation of a series, we generated {count} series with no trend, each with {length} yearly values, and ran the app's own trend test on every series: the Sen slope with its 95% interval and the Mann–Kendall test with the lag-1 Hamed–Rao correction. A series counts as a false alarm when the app would call it significant: p below {alpha} and a Sen interval that excludes zero. At this level, a perfect test would still raise a false alarm on {nominal} of trend-free series. The random seed, {seed}, was fixed before the run.
false_alarms.rule: Pass rule: at most {max} false alarms for r₁ up to {gated}. Higher r₁ values are reported separately, with no pass rule.
false_alarms.as_measured: Each rate is published as measured. A rate above the rule is marked as failed, and the check is never run again with another seed, length or estimator.
false_alarms.caption: False alarms on trend-free series, {count} series for each r₁
false_alarms.source: Source: {file}, written by the simulate command with engine version {version}.

data.heading: Data
data.model: Every trend on this site is computed from NASA POWER. POWER is model data, not observation: its weather values come from MERRA-2, a reanalysis that blends satellite and ground observations into a weather model to rebuild past weather.

station_check.heading: Station check: Phoenix hot days
station_check.label: NOAA station data, not NASA. Shown here as context only and never used in a verdict.
station_check.how: The Phoenix demo counts the days from May to October at or above 110 °F (43.3 °C) in one POWER grid cell. We counted the same days at the Phoenix Sky Harbor airport station (GHCN-Daily, {station}) for {first} to {last}, with no day missing, and ran the app's own trend test on both series.
station_check.caption: Days at or above 110 °F, May to October, {first} to {last}
station_check.agreement: Both trends rise, and the yearly counts correlate at r = {r}. With the trend line taken out of each series, r is still {detrended}, so the cell follows the station from year to year, not only in its trend.
station_check.gap: The cell counts about {gap} fewer such days a year than the station. One grid cell covers the city and the desert around it, so it cannot resolve a city's heat island.
station_check.source: Source: {file}, from GHCN-Daily station {station} (NOAA NCEI), computed with engine version {version}.

sources.heading: Sources and licenses
sources.intro: Every dataset, font, code package and paper that the app uses, with its license and how to cite it.

ai.heading: How AI is used
ai.note: AI produces no number on this site: the analysis service computes every number from NASA data, and this page shows saved evidence files. For a typed question, a language model may propose the variables, using catalog IDs only. Nothing runs until you confirm the proposal, and with the model switched off, a keyword match in English and Korean makes it. Every sentence that AI writes carries an AI badge. The code of this app was written with an AI coding assistant, Claude Code by Anthropic, and is checked by automated tests.
